screens.title: Capstone Project: Planning & Architecture
screens.narratorSegment: This chapter primes you to turn a mobile app idea into a deliverable capstone. We focus on the planning and architecture steps that dramatically increase the chance you’ll finish: defining a clear scope, choosing an appropriate framework, sketching wireframes, deciding how data is stored and synchronized, and establishing a Git workflow for collaboration. Think of planning as the foundation of a house: poor planning means a fragile structure, while a good plan keeps construction efficient and predictable. You will learn how to identify a Minimum Viable Product — the smallest set of features that delivers real value — and how to guard against scope creep by documenting essentials and deferring non-critical items. Practical choices follow: when to pick native development versus Flutter or React Native, how early wireframes save time, which local and remote data solutions fit different needs, and how version control practices protect your progress. For example, a simple recipe organizer MVP might need user accounts, add-recipe, and a searchable list — not video uploads or social feeds. As you proceed, ask: what is essential for first users, and what can wait? This orientation will keep your capstone realistic, testable, and ready for iterative improvement.

Capstone Project: Planning & Architecture

Establish a focused MVP, pick the right framework, design wireframes, define data strategy, and set a Git workflow that keeps your project manageable.

In this lesson

You’ll learn to scope an MVP, compare platform choices, sketch UI flows, choose local and remote data approaches, and set up Git for team work.

Concept Map
Core planning building blocks
MVP & Scope
Define the smallest useful feature set and non-functional targets.
Framework Choice
Pick native or cross-platform based on performance and timeline.
Data & Git
Choose local vs remote storage and a Git flow for collaboration.
Explore Key Topics
MVP Definition — Core features to ship first
Wireframing — Visualize user flow before coding
Data Strategy — Offline and sync trade-offs

screens.title: Defining Scope and the MVP
screens.narratorSegment: Defining scope begins with a clear problem statement: who you are building for and what they need. From there, brainstorm possible features, then apply the MVP lens: which features deliver the core value so users can perform the primary task? An MVP intentionally excludes secondary capabilities so you can launch early and learn. For example, a simple recipe organizer MVP might include user registration, adding and editing recipes, and a searchable recipe list. Features like video uploads, social sharing, or advanced filters are nice-to-haves for later. When documenting scope, also record non-functional requirements such as performance targets and basic security considerations; these guide architectural choices without expanding the feature list. A common misconception is that MVP means low quality. In truth, an MVP should be reliable and focused, not feature-heavy. Another pitfall is vague acceptance criteria: avoid it by writing concise success tests — for instance, a user can add a recipe and see it listed within two taps. Before moving to design, ask: what must exist in the first release to validate the idea? That question keeps scope disciplined and development predictable.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Define Scope & MVP
Definition

Minimum Viable Product

The smallest set of features that delivers the app's core value and allows early user feedback.

Example: Recipe Organizer
Essential: sign up, add recipe, search list. Defer: video uploads, social feeds.
Non-functional Requirements
Performance targets, basic security, and acceptable devices should be listed alongside features.
Key Takeaway

An MVP is focused and reliable — it tests the primary hypothesis without packing extraneous features.

Scope Decision Process
  1. Write a concise problem statement to clarify the primary user need.
  2. List all potential features and tag them as essential or deferred.
  3. Define success criteria for each essential feature to avoid ambiguity.
  4. Document non-functional targets that affect architecture or platform choice.
Common Mistake
Confusing MVP with a prototype. An MVP should be usable and meet acceptance criteria, not just a mock.
Acceptance Example
Success: A registered user can add a recipe and see it listed within two taps.

screens.title: Choosing a Framework
screens.narratorSegment: Framework choice affects development speed, performance, and long-term maintenance. Native iOS and Android offer the most direct access to platform APIs and highest performance for resource-intensive tasks, but they require separate codebases and more time to develop for both platforms. Flutter and React Native enable cross-platform development with a single codebase and faster iteration—often a pragmatic choice for simple to moderately complex apps. However, cross-platform frameworks introduce an abstraction layer that can complicate deep device integrations or extremely custom native UI behavior. When choosing, weigh your MVP needs: if your app is a simple utility or content-driven product, Flutter or React Native lets you reach both platforms quickly. If your capstone demands advanced device features, tight performance budgets, or platform-specific UX, native development may be preferable. Also consider your own or your team's experience: familiarity reduces risk. A common misconception is that cross-platform always saves time; in practice, complex native integrations can negate that advantage. Close by asking: which framework minimizes friction for your MVP while meeting performance and integration requirements? Choosing a Framework means select a framework based on required performance, device integration, development speed, and team expertise.. In practical terms, native ios/android vs flutter vs react native. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Framework Selection
Comparison

Native vs Cross-platform

Native iOS / Android
Best performance and API access; separate code for each platform.
Flutter
Fast cross-platform UI with a single codebase; strong for consistent design.
React Native
Cross-platform with JS ecosystem; good for rapid iterations on standard UIs.
When to pick native
Performance-critical apps or deep native integrations.
When to pick cross-platform
Rapid delivery to both platforms for simpler feature sets.
Decision Checklist
  • Does the MVP require advanced native APIs?
  • What is the timeline and budget?
  • What expertise does the team have?
  • Is UI consistency or platform-specific look more important?
Quick Example
A simple habit tracker can often use Flutter or React Native for speed; a game or low-level tool often favors native.

screens.title: Wireframing & Mockups
screens.narratorSegment: Wireframing is a low-cost way to validate layout and user flow before writing UI code. Start with a sketch of the main screens for your core flow — for example, a main list, an add-item screen, and a detail screen. These low-fidelity wireframes focus on layout and navigation, not colors or typography. After validating with peers or users, create higher-fidelity mockups that show exact placement, spacing, and visual hierarchy. Mockups communicate the visual design you plan to implement and help catch usability issues like crowded controls or unclear navigation. Tools like Figma, Adobe XD, or even pen and paper are acceptable; the important part is iteration. A common misconception is that designers must be professional to wireframe — they don't. Simple sketches reveal major usability issues faster than code. As a practical process: sketch the flow, test it briefly with a peer, convert the most important screen to a mockup, and note any changes required for the implementation plan. Ask yourself: does this flow let users achieve the core task with minimal friction? Wireframing & Mockups means wireframes expose flow problems cheaply; mockups clarify design details before code is written.. In practical terms, from low-fidelity sketches to visual mockups. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Wireframing & Mockups
Process

Sketch → Validate → Mockup

Step 1: Sketch
Draw core screens for the primary flow using pen or low-fi tool.
Step 2: Validate
Test sketches with a peer or potential user to catch flow issues early.
Step 3: Mockup
Build higher-fidelity mockups for the screens that matter most to implementation.
Example Flow: Habit Tracker
Main List
Shows habits with quick toggles and progress.
Add Habit
Minimal fields: title, frequency, reminder toggle.
Habit Detail
Shows history and edit controls.
Pro Tip
Keep each wireframe to one task; cluttered screens hide usability issues.

screens.title: Data Management Strategy
screens.narratorSegment: A data management strategy answers where and how your app stores user data. For offline-first needs, local persistence such as SQLite, Room on Android, or Core Data on iOS is essential. For multi-device synchronization and cloud features, remote databases like a managed BaaS or a custom REST A P I are necessary. Many apps benefit from a hybrid approach: store data locally for instant access and synchronize with a remote database for cross-device consistency. For example, a notes app should let users access notes offline using local persistence and then sync changes to a remote database so they appear on other devices. When planning APIs, design clear data models and consider authentication requirements like token-based approaches. Also plan for conflict resolution when simultaneous edits occur — a simple strategy is last-write-wins or merging based on timestamps, but document this as part of your architecture. A common misconception is that cloud sync replaces local storage; in practice, local storage improves responsiveness and supports offline use. Your documentation should state which data is stored locally, what sync triggers exist, and basic error handling for network failures.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Data Management Strategy
Definition

Local, Remote, or Hybrid?

Decide where each piece of data lives and how updates flow between device and server.
Local Options
iOS: Core Data; Android: Room/SQLite; alternatives: Realm.
Remote Options
BaaS like Firebase or a custom REST/GraphQL backend for sync and sharing.
Hybrid Strategy Example
Notes app: local storage for offline access, sync to cloud for multi-device access. Specify sync triggers and conflict resolution rules.
Sync Considerations
When to push changes, conflict handling, and network error strategies.
Authentication
Plan token-based auth or OAuth where needed and document how tokens are stored and refreshed.
Key Takeaway

Prioritize local persistence for responsiveness; add remote sync when multi-device access or backups are required.

screens.title: API Integration & Data Models
screens.narratorSegment: A P I integration ties your mobile UI to backend services. Start by modeling the data your app needs — entities, attributes, and relationships — before designing endpoints. Clear data models simplify serialization and mapping to local storage schemas. For a simple social feed or notes app, models might include User, Item, and Timestamp. Design endpoints that support the MVP operations: create, read, update, delete, and list with simple query parameters. Authentication should be planned early: token-based approaches like JSON Web Tokens or OAuth flows are common; document how tokens are stored, refreshed, and invalidated. Also plan for error handling and retries on network failures. A common misconception is that the backend can be an afterthought; in reality, A P I design influences client complexity and UI decisions. Sketch a minimal A P I surface: which endpoints are essential for your MVP, what payloads they use, and what status codes mean success or failure. This reduces integration ambiguity and speeds development when front-end and back-end are built in parallel. API Integration & Data Models means define data models first, then design minimal endpoints and authentication so the client and server align cleanly.. In practical terms, designing models, endpoints, and basic auth flow. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › API Integration
Architecture

Data Models and Endpoints

Define entities, then map to endpoints that support only the MVP operations.
Model Example
User {id, name}; Note {id, userId, content, updatedAt}
Essential Endpoints
/notes GET, POST, PUT, DELETE and /auth/login
Auth & Error Handling
Plan token lifecycle, storage, and refresh. Define retry rules and user-facing messages for common network errors.
Integration Checklist
  • Data model doc
  • Essential endpoints defined
  • Auth flow documented
  • Basic error and retry strategy

screens.title: Version Control with Git
screens.narratorSegment: Version control is essential for any capstone. Initialize a Git repository early and host it remotely so your work is preserved and shareable. Learn and use core commands: initialize the repo, add and commit changes, push and pull, and create branches for features. Adopt a simple branching strategy: create a feature branch for each new capability and merge it into main after review and testing. This prevents accidental changes from landing in the main codebase and makes it easy to revert if needed. For example, create feature/login-ui to add a login screen and merge via pull request. Also document repository structure and where key files live. A common misconception is that Git is only for teams; even solo projects benefit from commits and branches. Keep commits focused and descriptive; each commit should represent a logical change. If you need to show commands in the repo README, include examples and a short workflow: create branch, develop, commit, open a pull request, review, and merge. This structure keeps your capstone reproducible and reviewable. Version Control with Git means use feature branches and clear commits to keep work reversible and collaborative, even for solo capstones.. In practical terms, repository setup, essential commands, and branching strategy. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Git Workflow
Code Walkthrough

Initialize and Branch

Example commands you might include in your README to help reviewers or collaborators.

git init
git add .
git commit -m "chore: initial commit"

git branch -m main
git remote add origin <remote-repo-url>
git push -u origin main

# Create a feature branch
git checkout -b feature/user-profile
# Work, then
git add .
git commit -m "feat: add user profile screen"
git push -u origin feature/user-profile
Branching Strategy
Use a simple feature-branch workflow: develop in branches, open pull requests for review, merge to main when ready. Keep main deployable.
Common Mistake
Working directly on main increases risk of regressions and makes rebasing harder. Avoid it.

screens.title: Repository Structure & Collaboration
screens.narratorSegment: A sensible repository structure reduces onboarding friction and eases navigation for reviewers. At minimum, organize your project into folders for source code, assets, and documentation. Include a README that describes the project idea, MVP, how to run the app locally, and where wireframes live. Use a simple branching convention such as feature/* for work-in-progress and main for production-ready code. For collaboration, use pull requests with clear descriptions and link the PR to the related milestone or issue. If you need to demonstrate CI or tests, include a minimal pipeline that runs linting or unit tests before merging. A frequent misconception is that a capstone repo must mirror a production repo; instead, focus on clarity: a reviewer should be able to run the app and find the core files quickly. Also include a changelog or short release notes so incremental progress is visible. Document conventions for commit messages and code style so reviewers can focus on functional correctness instead of style differences. Repository Structure & Collaboration means a clear repo structure, readme, and branching rules make the project easier to run, review, and maintain.. In practical terms, organize files and collaborate with feature branches. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Handling Scope Creep
screens.narratorSegment: Scope creep appears when new features are added during development without reconsidering time or resources. To control scope creep, record every requested change and classify it: is it essential for the MVP, or a future enhancement? Use a backlog with priority tags and enforce a rule: only items classified as MVP may be implemented for the initial release. Another effective technique is time-boxing: allocate fixed time windows for building features and stop when the window closes. Keep a visible list of deferred items labeled as 'nice-to-have' so they are not forgotten but also not obscuring immediate goals. Also establish acceptance criteria for each feature to avoid ambiguity in completion. A common misconception is that adding more features improves the product; early users often prefer clarity and reliability. Regularly review scope with stakeholders or peers and say no to feature expansion that jeopardizes the release timeline. At the end, ask yourself: does this change help validate the core user need now, or should it wait? screens.title: Practical Tips & Common Pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: A few practical habits will make your capstone smoother. First, keep feature tickets small and focused so each can be completed and reviewed quickly. Second, use short, descriptive commit messages that explain why a change was made, not just what changed. Third, automate simple checks like linting to catch style issues early. Fourth, keep wireframes and notes in the repository or docs folder so everything reviewers need is in one place. Common pitfalls include over-engineering the first release, delaying Git initialization, and failing to document acceptance criteria. Another frequent mistake is underestimating time for testing on actual devices; allocate time for real-device checks, not just simulators. If you run into integration issues with third-party services, fall back to stubbing responses so you can continue building UI. These small practices reduce friction and keep the capstone on track. Finally, schedule short peer reviews to get early feedback before large features are merged. fullNarratorScript:
This chapter primes you to turn a mobile app idea into a deliverable capstone. We focus on the planning and architecture steps that dramatically increase the chance you’ll finish: defining a clear scope, choosing an appropriate framework, sketching wireframes, deciding how data is stored and synchronized, and establishing a Git workflow for collaboration. Think of planning as the foundation of a house: poor planning means a fragile structure, while a good plan keeps construction efficient and predictable. You will learn how to identify a Minimum Viable Product — the smallest set of features that delivers real value — and how to guard against scope creep by documenting essentials and deferring non-critical items. Practical choices follow: when to pick native development versus Flutter or React Native, how early wireframes save time, which local and remote data solutions fit different needs, and how version control practices protect your progress. For example, a simple recipe organizer MVP might need user accounts, add-recipe, and a searchable list — not video uploads or social feeds. As you proceed, ask: what is essential for first users, and what can wait? This orientation will keep your capstone realistic, testable, and ready for iterative improvement.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to define a focused MVP and document core features so your capstone remains achievable. You will assess trade-offs between native iOS, native Android, Flutter, and React Native and choose the framework that best matches your project constraints and skills. You will create basic wireframes and mockups that capture user flows and critical screens, allowing you to spot usability issues early. You will also outline a data management plan that chooses local persistence, remote synchronization, or a hybrid approach based on offline needs and multi-device sync. Finally, you will set up a robust Git workflow and repository structure so collaboration, feature branching, and release management are reliable. Each objective includes a short mnemonic or visual cue to help you remember the skill and a verified competency milestone to mark readiness to proceed.

This second objectives slide focuses on practical deliverables you will produce. First, you will write a concise problem statement that clarifies who your app serves and what primary problem it solves. This improves prioritization when picking MVP features. Second, you will produce a 3–5 item MVP feature list and identify 2–3 nice-to-have features to defer. Third, you will choose and justify a framework—explain why native or cross-platform best supports your MVP. Finally, you will produce simple wireframes for the core user flow and add a basic Git repository configured with at least one feature branch. Each deliverable maps directly to a milestone: problem statement, MVP list, framework justification, wireframe artifacts, and an initialized Git repo. These concrete outputs are what reviewers and peers look for when assessing your capstone readiness.

Defining scope begins with a clear problem statement: who you are building for and what they need. From there, brainstorm possible features, then apply the MVP lens: which features deliver the core value so users can perform the primary task? An MVP intentionally excludes secondary capabilities so you can launch early and learn. For example, a simple recipe organizer MVP might include user registration, adding and editing recipes, and a searchable recipe list. Features like video uploads, social sharing, or advanced filters are nice-to-haves for later. When documenting scope, also record non-functional requirements such as performance targets and basic security considerations; these guide architectural choices without expanding the feature list. A common misconception is that MVP means low quality. In truth, an MVP should be reliable and focused, not feature-heavy. Another pitfall is vague acceptance criteria: avoid it by writing concise success tests — for instance, a user can add a recipe and see it listed within two taps. Before moving to design, ask: what must exist in the first release to validate the idea? That question keeps scope disciplined and development predictable.

Framework choice affects development speed, performance, and long-term maintenance. Native iOS and Android offer the most direct access to platform APIs and highest performance for resource-intensive tasks, but they require separate codebases and more time to develop for both platforms. Flutter and React Native enable cross-platform development with a single codebase and faster iteration—often a pragmatic choice for simple to moderately complex apps. However, cross-platform frameworks introduce an abstraction layer that can complicate deep device integrations or extremely custom native UI behavior. When choosing, weigh your MVP needs: if your app is a simple utility or content-driven product, Flutter or React Native lets you reach both platforms quickly. If your capstone demands advanced device features, tight performance budgets, or platform-specific UX, native development may be preferable. Also consider your own or your team's experience: familiarity reduces risk. A common misconception is that cross-platform always saves time; in practice, complex native integrations can negate that advantage. Close by asking: which framework minimizes friction for your MVP while meeting performance and integration requirements? Choosing a Framework means select a framework based on required performance, device integration, development speed, and team expertise.. Wireframing is a low-cost way to validate layout and user flow before writing UI code. Start with a sketch of the main screens for your core flow — for example, a main list, an add-item screen, and a detail screen. These low-fidelity wireframes focus on layout and navigation, not colors or typography. After validating with peers or users, create higher-fidelity mockups that show exact placement, spacing, and visual hierarchy. Mockups communicate the visual design you plan to implement and help catch usability issues like crowded controls or unclear navigation. Tools like Figma, Adobe XD, or even pen and paper are acceptable; the important part is iteration. A common misconception is that designers must be professional to wireframe — they don't. Simple sketches reveal major usability issues faster than code. A data management strategy answers where and how your app stores user data. For offline-first needs, local persistence such as SQLite, Room on Android, or Core Data on iOS is essential. For multi-device synchronization and cloud features, remote databases like a managed BaaS or a custom REST A P I are necessary. Many apps benefit from a hybrid approach: store data locally for instant access and synchronize with a remote database for cross-device consistency. For example, a notes app should let users access notes offline using local persistence and then sync changes to a remote database so they appear on other devices. When planning APIs, design clear data models and consider authentication requirements like token-based approaches. Also plan for conflict resolution when simultaneous edits occur — a simple strategy is last-write-wins or merging based on timestamps, but document this as part of your architecture. A common misconception is that cloud sync replaces local storage; in practice, local storage improves responsiveness and supports offline use. Your documentation should state which data is stored locally, what sync triggers exist, and basic error handling for network failures.

A P I integration ties your mobile UI to backend services. Start by modeling the data your app needs — entities, attributes, and relationships — before designing endpoints. Clear data models simplify serialization and mapping to local storage schemas. For a simple social feed or notes app, models might include User, Item, and Timestamp. Design endpoints that support the MVP operations: create, read, update, delete, and list with simple query parameters. Authentication should be planned early: token-based approaches like JSON Web Tokens or OAuth flows are common; document how tokens are stored, refreshed, and invalidated. Also plan for error handling and retries on network failures. A common misconception is that the backend can be an afterthought; in reality, A P I design influences client complexity and UI decisions. Sketch a minimal A P I surface: which endpoints are essential for your MVP, what payloads they use, and what status codes mean success or failure. This reduces integration ambiguity and speeds development when front-end and back-end are built in parallel.
